title: Arrays, indices and ranges
body: An array is a fixed-length, zero-indexed block of elements of one type: `int[] scores = new int[3];` creates three zeros, because new arrays hold each element type's default value (0, false, null). A collection expression `int[] primes = [2, 3, 5];` creates and fills one. Arrays are reference types, so assigning an array variable aliases it.

Indexing checks bounds at runtime: `scores[3]` on a three-element array throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`. `Length` gives the element count. `^1` is an index from the end, so `primes[^1]` is the last element. A range `a[1..3]` creates a new array containing indices 1 and 2; the end is exclusive.

Multidimensional arrays `int[,] grid = new int[2, 3];` are rectangular and indexed `grid[row, col]`, with `GetLength(0)` and `GetLength(1)` for sizes. Jagged arrays `int[][]` are arrays of arrays whose rows may differ in length; each row must be created separately.

`Array.Sort`, `Array.Reverse`, `Array.IndexOf` and `Array.Fill` work in place. `Array.Copy` and `CopyTo` duplicate elements; `Clone()` makes a shallow copy (the elements of a reference-type array still alias the same objects). Use `List<T>` (stage 6) when the size changes.

A range on an array copies, while a range on a span (stage 10) is a view without copying. Before slicing, check whether you need an independent copy or a view of the same memory, and remember that an out-of-range index is a runtime failure, not a compile error.
challenge: Given int[] values = [3, 8, 1, 9, 4], print the last two elements using a range from the end, then rotate the array left by one in place and print it.
question: What does `primes[1..4]` produce for an int[] in C#?
correct: A new array with the elements at indices 1, 2 and 3
wrong: A view sharing the original array's storage
reasoning: Range ends are exclusive, and slicing an array allocates a copy; use AsSpan() for a non-copying view.
